claims.text: High-entropy or multi-principal-element alloys use at least five principal elements.
Refractory HEAs can comprise elements such as W, Mo, Ta, Nb, and V and are relevant to elevated-temperature applications.
RHEAs can occur as BCC solid solutions or BCC+B2 microstructures.
Multiple elements with different atomic sizes cause atoms in HEAs to deviate from ideal lattice sites, producing local lattice distortion.
Severe local lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Severe local lattice distortion alters the thermodynamic stability of RHEAs.
The vast compositional space of HEAs creates a need for efficient computational design and screening tools.
CALPHAD has an important role in HEA design and requires both computational software and a thermodynamic database.
A workflow that first identifies stable phases using CALPHAD and then applies a machine-learned lattice-distortion surrogate can predict fusion enthalpy and melting temperature.
The surrogate workflow can bypass first-principles calculations for every composition.
First-principles calculations become computationally prohibitive in quinary and higher-order systems because calculation time scales with the number of components.
The proposed methodology is intended for refractory alloys at temperatures above 1000 K.
High configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion stabilize RHEA solid solutions against melting.
Lattice-distortion magnitude is correlated with the energy barrier for melting.
The lattice-distortion correlation permits prediction of melting properties without full liquid-state dynamics for every composition.
The hybrid method will predict melting temperature and entropy of fusion within 5% of experimental benchmarks or theoretical limits.
The hybrid method will reduce computational time from thousands of hours to a few hours per system.
Pure CALPHAD screening of a quinary system at 1 at.% resolution takes thousands of hours.
CALPHAD alone struggles to predict melting properties in severely distorted systems without extensive experimental database inputs.

The method is valid for refractory single-phase BCC or BCC+B2 systems but may fail for complex intermetallic precipitation, non-equilibrium phases, or compositions outside the surrogate's training domain.
